[h1][b]🎮 Reseña de Virtual Rides 3 - Funfair Simulator[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Virtual Rides 3 - Funfair Simulator es básicamente un “parque de diversiones de bolsillo” en modo simulador casual: te subes a atracciones, paseas por el recinto como si fueras inspector de seguridad con complejo de turista y te dedicas a probar la física (a veces más de la cuenta) mientras el juego intenta convencerte de que esto es “relajación” y “para toda la familia”.

La primera impresión es clara: esto no viene a contarte una historia épica ni a retarte con sistemas profundos; viene a darte una experiencia de feria, con enfoque en simulación ligera, paseo y sensación inmersiva. Y sí, tiene soporte RV… porque nada dice “diversión” como marearte voluntariamente en una atracción virtual sin el algodón de azúcar para compensar.

[h2][b]🎡 Lo que Sube la Adrenalina vs. Lo que Te Baja del Juego[/b][/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ Física presente y protagonista 🤹‍♂️ (cuando funciona, se siente como “simulador” de verdad)  
✅ Soporte RV 🥽 (ideal para quien quiera feria sin salir de casa)  
✅ Modificables 🧩 (si te gusta meter mano y alargarle la vida, hay carnita)  
✅ Steam Cloud ☁️ (porque hasta tus paseos merecen respaldo)  
✅ Logros y cromos 🏆🃏 (dopamina rápida para completistas)

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ Comunidad actual diminuta 👻 (3 jugadores: esto es más una reunión familiar que un fenómeno)  
❌ Experiencia principalmente de un jugador 🚶‍♂️ (si buscabas caos con amigos, aquí solo te acompaña el viento)  
❌ Sensación “casual” por encima de “simulador profundo” 🧸 (si eres exigente, se te puede quedar corto)  
❌ Solo 10 logros 🎯 (se acaban antes que la fila de la montaña rusa en martes)  
❌ “Realista” hasta que te acuerdas que estás en un simulador de feria 😅 (la inmersión depende mucho de tus expectativas)

Virtual Rides 3, developed by Pixelsplit Simulations, offers a unique and immersive experience for players who’ve ever dreamed of running their own fairground. Rather than focusing on the business aspects of a theme park simulator, this game places its attention squarely on the heart of the carnival: the rides themselves. It’s a love letter to the sights, sounds, and sensations of the funfair, letting players take control of every flashing light, rotating seat, and booming speaker. From operating massive pendulum rides to customizing laser shows and fog machines, Virtual Rides 3 is about showmanship and spectacle, and it delivers this in spades.

At the core of the experience is the ability to operate rides in real-time. Each ride is impressively modeled with a control booth interface that mirrors real-life amusement park machinery. Players aren’t simply clicking a “Start” button; they’re managing speeds, music, lighting, loading sequences, safety procedures, and timing. This hands-on approach makes running each ride feel like a performance rather than just a task. It’s especially satisfying during night cycles, where lighting effects really come to life, turning your custom fairground into a visually stunning festival of color and motion. The game offers more than fifteen rides in its base version, with several others available via downloadable content, providing a nice variety of thrill levels, from slow family attractions to high-intensity pendulum and spinning arm rides.

Customization is one of the strongest aspects of Virtual Rides 3. Each ride can be modified with different paint jobs, light sequences, soundtracks, and special effects like lasers and fog. This adds an incredible degree of personal expression to the experience. Players can build and arrange their fairground layout, place food stalls, props, and decorative elements to shape the vibe of the entire event. Whether you want a retro carnival look, a futuristic dance-club aesthetic, or a moody night market ambiance, the tools are here. It's clear that the developers aimed to make the game not just a simulator, but a digital playground for creativity.

The crowd system, while not deeply simulated in terms of behavior or economic feedback, serves the atmosphere well. Visitors wander the fairgrounds, cheer when rides start, react to the lighting and audio, and give a sense of life to your creation. It’s more about immersion than management. This lack of financial or managerial mechanics may disappoint players coming from traditional park sims, but Virtual Rides 3 isn’t trying to be RollerCoaster Tycoon. It’s more akin to a ride enthusiast’s toolkit—something to enjoy slowly and artistically, without the pressure of spreadsheets or competition.

Visually, the game does a solid job, especially considering its niche focus. The models for rides are detailed and well-animated, and lighting effects are genuinely impressive when used creatively. The day-night cycle adds an extra layer of charm, especially when combined with custom light shows. Though not pushing the boundaries of modern graphics, the stylized presentation is effective and atmospheric. Performance-wise, the game is stable on most systems, with optimization that keeps frame rates steady even when the fairground gets crowded with guests and lighting effects.

Some weaknesses do exist, especially in terms of interface and complexity. The controls for setting up and configuring effects can be a bit clunky at first, and new players may find the menus overwhelming. Building placement sometimes feels finicky, especially when trying to arrange multiple rides and decorations in a tight space. Additionally, while DLC adds more rides and props, the base game can start to feel a bit repetitive if you don't invest in the extra content. It’s clear that the long-term value of the game is tied closely to how much time players are willing to spend mastering the tools and making the most out of customization features.

Despite these minor drawbacks, Virtual Rides 3 succeeds as a specialized, creative sandbox that captures the magic of a fairground in a way few other games attempt. It’s a game that knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers on that promise with confidence. For players who appreciate amusement rides, enjoy crafting immersive environments, or simply want to experience what it’s like to run a carnival from the operator’s booth, this game offers hours of satisfying, hands-on fun. It might not have the broad appeal of a tycoon sim, but for its target audience, it’s a thrilling and personal celebration of the art of the ride.

I bought this game mainly for the VR experiences, but unfortunately, they’re quite underwhelming.
Some of the experiences are sold separately as DLC, which I haven’t tested.

As far as VR is concerned, every experience ended with the thought… “Is that it?” or failed to provide any real satisfaction.
Moreover, many of the experiences have major issues with positioning. Often, after resetting the view, you end up 20 cm above the seat or a meter off, sometimes even in front of or between the seats. This further breaks immersion, as you have to reset the view and physically move yourself into the right position while wearing the headset – which is often not physically possible.

Just to be clear, I’m not reviewing the whole game, only what it offers for VR users.
If, like me, you’re interested specifically in the VR experiences, I’d advise against purchasing.

Feedback for Virtual Rides 3 – Accessibility and keyboard control for visually impaired players

Dear developers,

I am visually impaired and I really enjoy playing Virtual Rides 3. I would like to suggest a few improvements that would make the game more accessible and easier to control without relying on vision:
	1.	Automatic closing of safety bars:
In the Hurricane (Breakdance), the staff member collects tickets and closes the safety bars, which helps me know when the ride is full. In other rides like the Tentacle, the staff only collects tickets, and I have to close the safety bars myself — but I can’t see when everyone is seated. It would help to have an option for automatic safety bar closing, or at least a sound or voice cue when the ride is full.
	2.	Keyboard control for music:
Right now, only jingles can be controlled with the keyboard. Please consider adding keyboard shortcuts like Insert to turn the music on/off, and Home/End to browse tracks.
	3.	Keyboard navigation for the map:
After pressing Escape to open the map, everything must be done with the mouse. It would be much more accessible if I could use arrow keys to move between rides and Enter to select one.

Thank you for considering these changes. They would make the game much more accessible to visually impaired players like me.

Best regards,
Renzo
